extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, and readers of political philosophy interested in constitutions and forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing, classifying, and designing constitutions and polities (democracies, oligarchies, aristocracies, tyrannies), with concrete institutional recommendations about assemblies, magistracies, census, and mixtures of forms. Useful to legislators, political theorists, and students of classical political thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme power should rest in the law rather than in men
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constituted state places the supreme power in the law (not in particular persons); when the multitude or the poor dominate for other reasons, supreme power tends to reside in men rather than the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts regimes where the law rules (common in moderate-property oligarchies) with those where men rule (e.g., certain democracies where the poor, by their numbers and wages for attendance, effectively hold power). The criterion implies preferring institutional arrangements that secure the rule of law over rule by personalities or factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify regimes by property distribution and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and species of oligarchy or democracy depend on how property is distributed and on the relative numbers of rich, poor, and middling citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., many citizens of moderate property -> power in laws; few with very large fortunes -> oligarchy of the second sort; progressively concentrated wealth -> oligarchy → dynastic oligarchy → monarchy. Use property and numerical relations to diagnose regime type and predict likely evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy: government by the best on virtuous principles
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy properly is a state governed by the best men upon the most virtuous principles; only there is a man both a good man and a good citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes true aristocracy (virtue-centered) from forms named 'aristocracy' that simply include the rich or the virtuous; judges regimes by whether honour accrues to virtue rather than to wealth or hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: A free state should be a balanced mixture of democracy and oligarchy (a medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: A free state is essentially a mixture of democratic and oligarchical elements; the best constitution approximates a medium between extremes rather than an extreme form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three blending methods are proposed (adopt rules common to both, take a median between opposing practices such as census size, or adopt different laws from each to create a hybrid). The best proof of a successful mixture is that the state may legitimately be called both democracy and oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be good and effectively enforced; they must suit the governed
rubrics_metrics.description: A good constitution requires not only good laws but also that such laws are observed and fitted to those who must abide by them (either best relative to the particular state or best absolutely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two signs of a good constitution: (1) enforcement/obedience to its laws, and (2) laws well calculated for the citizens. A law ill-suited to its people will produce obedience but be unjust or unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor the middle (middling) class for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle rank (moderately well-off citizens) produces the most stable, law-abiding, and moderate polity; a state composed principally of this middle class is politically best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremes (very rich or very poor) produce caprice, faction, and insubordination. Legislators should aim to make the middle class numerous and respectable; many of the best lawgivers historically came from the middle rank (Solon, Lycurgus, Charondas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators should design constitutions to empower the middle rank
rubrics_metrics.description: When framing constitutions, special regard must be given to the middling sort: if an oligarchy is intended the laws should focus on them; if a democracy they should be entrusted to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The middle rank acts as an arbitrator acceptable to rich and poor; constitutions grounded on a robust middle class better resist collusion of rich and poor and reduce the likelihood of sedition or tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend institutions by (1) adopting common rules, (2) taking a medium, or (3) mixing distinct laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Three explicit procedures for composing a mixed constitution: adopt rules common to both regimes; take a middle position between opposing practices (e.g., census size); borrow different laws from each form (e.g., elect some magistrates by vote and others by lot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: judicial attendance payments, voting by lot vs vote, census thresholds. A successful blend preserves recognizable elements of both forms and prevents either extreme from dominating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship should be tied to bearing arms (military qualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizens of a free state ought to consist of those who bear arms; in some states power also belongs to those who have borne them (veterans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for linking political rights and public duties to military service; historically many Greek states limited citizenship to the armed or veteran class. This shapes who participates in assemblies and holds magistracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the census as extensive as possible so enrolled citizens form the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: The census or enrollment for political rights should be made as extensive as possible so that those enrolled make up a greater part of the people than those who are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad census helps stability because poorer citizens who are enrolled and have a stake are more willing to live quiet lives and defend the state. But practical limits exist and behavior of ruling elites matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalize pay and fines for civic duties across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent oligarchic trickery and democratic imbalance, extend both the pay for attendance and fines for non-attendance to all classes equally (or apply both pay and fine to every member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle identifies oligarchic contrivances (fining only the rich, paying only the poor) and democratic contrivances (paying the poor only). Equalized incentives/penalties encourage universal participation and prevent avoidance or manipulation of enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and assign the powers of the public assembly clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper business of the public assembly should include war and peace, alliances, enacting laws, capital sentences, banishment, confiscation, and holding magistrates accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether such powers are entrusted to all citizens, one magistrate, some magistrates, or divided among bodies. The scope of assembly powers distinguishes democracies from other forms and must be matched to institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose among explicit methods to vest deliberative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberative power may be vested by rotation (all serve in turn), by a supreme council of magistrates, by collective assemblies limited to certain functions, or by full participatory deliberation (pure democracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method suits different sizes and characters of state: rotation and councils suit large states with many offices; collective assemblies for comitia; pure democracy requires small polities. Match method to practical scale and civic competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design democratic institutions to hold frequent assemblies and balance class representation
rubrics_metrics.description: In a democracy, frequent assemblies are advantageous; poor should be rewarded for attendance; councils should include equal numbers of nobles and citizens or otherwise balance ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the common people are very numerous, either pay only enough to equalise them with nobles or select many by lot to participate. These techniques prevent numerical dominance from producing disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design oligarchical institutions to give limited inclusion to common people
rubrics_metrics.description: In an oligarchy, call some common people to councils or establish advisory/pre-advisory bodies; allow the people limited voting (e.g., vote but not propose) to involve them without ceding disruptive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include 'pre-advisers' who propose before formal enactment, giving the people a vote on proposals but not initiative, or giving pardon-power but not condemnation. These arrangements reduce the risk of popular disorder while preserving some legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate pardoning and condemning powers appropriate to regime type
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to pardon or condemn should be assigned in ways that fit the regime: democracies should have pardoning power with magistrates retaining condemnation, while republics (few ruling) should reverse this allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allocation is a tool for balancing authority and preventing abuses; refer difficult or dangerous powers to magistrates when mass decisions are risky, or to the people when magistrates are few and liable to abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design magistracies with attention to number, office, term length, reappointment, eligibility and appointment method
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing magistrates consider how many offices there should be, the particular functions, the term durations (six months, a year, perpetual, etc.), reappointment rules, eligibility, and whether selection is by vote, lot, or other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different choices suit different regimes and sizes of state. Term length affects accountability and stability; eligibility/census affects class composition of officeholders; method of appointment (vote/lot) shapes the character of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish civil magistrates from priests/ceremonial roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every elected or chosen official should be called a magistrate; priests, choregi, heralds, ambassadors, and servile economic officers differ from true magistrates (those who deliberate, decide causes, or command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate classification matters for institutional design: focus on offices that carry deliberative authority, judicial functions, or command when designing rotations, eligibility, and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign single specialized employment in large states; combine offices in small states
rubrics_metrics.description: In extensive governments it is proper to allot one employment to one person; in small states fewer people necessitate combining several employments in the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration of attention improves performance in large polities; in small polities, combining offices is sometimes necessary and acceptable provided duties do not conflict. Consider population size when structuring offices and rotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and guard against the five oligarchic contrivances of the rich
rubrics_metrics.description: The rich attempt, under fair pretences, to undermine popular rights via five channels: public assemblies (penalizing or not), offices (allowing poor to shirk), courts of justice (unequal fines), military power, and gymnastic exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and counteract such contrivances by equalizing obligations and benefits, broadening enrollment, and ensuring the rich cannot manipulate attendance or qualifications to exclude rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify three species of tyranny to diagnose and prevent them
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrannies include: (1) kingly power regulated by law (monarchic), (2) despotism ruling according to will, and (3) a ruler who governs equals/superiors without accountability for his own advantage and by compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these types helps legislators recognize when a monarchy verges toward tyranny and to design checks (accountability, law) to prevent the emergence of the third kind, which is most antithetical to freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure constitutional stability by making preservation internal
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-composed mixed state should have its means of preservation in itself — citizens should not wish the least alteration in the constitution because they are invested in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional stability comes from internal consent and balanced interests (especially a strong middle rank), not from external guarantees or the forbearance of neighbours; design institutions that create local incentives to preserve the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance 'quality' (liberty, riches, education, family) with 'quantity' (populousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every city is made up of quality (liberty, riches, education, family) and quantity (population); quality and quantity may exist in different parts and must be properly adjusted to each other to prevent regime change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quantity of a lower-quality class (e.g., poor, ignoble) exceeds a higher-quality minority, a democracy or oligarchy of a particular class may arise; legislators should calibrate institutions (census, eligibility, representation) to maintain balance.
